utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrbic. Welcome back to the courtroom. Please be reminded that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. McCloskey is continuing his cross-examination. You have the floor, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General. And I think we left off with P2520 up there, the 12 of July document. That was the request to the ministry for the mobilisation of the buses. And as I recall it, general, you received a verbal request from someone from the Main Staff the night before this actual request, and then you spoke to someone from the ministry and they wanted you to get it on paper. So on the morning of the 12th, you had this typed off and sent it off. Is that roughly correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so the night of the 11th when you got this call, can you just roughly give us any idea of about what time it was or was it after dinner, was it late, was it before you ate? Any recollection about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, my memory is not fresh, but it was certainly in the afternoon and most probably in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for a moment can we go to P1744.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is, I think, one of those aerials you were mentioning where we have a date. Unfortunately, we don't have a time for this. But we see it's Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we zero-in on the centre of that -- right there, yes. Where the marking is. Yeah, right up in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see -- I can tell you, sir, that Mr. Ruez and others have identified -- we see -- stay there for one second. The football stadium of Bratunac is up in the right-hand corner. You can sort of barely make out that big field area with bushes around it. And as we go to the left, yes, right there where the arrow is, that's the football stadium. And as we go towards the left on the main road in the dark -- yeah, keep going, good, good, and then down. Right there where that arrow is, that's a line of buses on the 12th of July. So it appears that your request, your oral request, and your follow-up request was acted on very efficiently. And we've also seen video on the 12th of July with General Krstic giving an interview [where there's buses going by. So to your recollection, were buses able to get to the stadium on the 12th of July, or are you learning it from me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I've heard about this from Mr. McCloskey because I didn't monitor the implementation of our request to the ministry of Republika Srpska. As you saw in the previous documents, the Secretariats of Defence had to report to the Ministry of Defence. The Ministry of Defence did not have to report to the Main Staff on the manner in which our request for the mobilisation of buses had been carried out. Your Honours, I didn't have the responsibility to monitor the movement of buses -- of those buses. This aerial photograph, Mr. McCloskey, clearly shows that these are some kinds of vehicles. And if you enlarge them, they couldn't be anything but buses. That's probably the case. But some look like trailers. An expert for analysing such photographs - and you certainly had such an expert - would be in a position to provide you with more relevant comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, if this -- as everyone knows, as you've said yesterday, this is General Mladic's request for buses for the army, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you -- who in the army would be responsible for monitoring that this order would be carried out and to dealing with -- with the buses? Certainly informing General Mladic and others whether this was happening.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army, the operations centre would be responsible for monitoring the situation, but on the roads themselves, Your Honours, it's the civilian police, the traffic police, and the military police to a certain extent that escort this convoy. Since this road was a threat from combat activity, there was also security that was provided for that column but that was indirect support. Some units were at their positions - I can't name them - and they protected those roads. And the military police also provided direct protection for the roads so that the buses could reach their destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I was asking about who in the Main Staff, and so you're saying it's operations, so it's General Miletic's operation that would have been in charge of monitoring this request and implementing it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a duty officer in the operations centre who leads the operations team. General Miletic couldn't do that all the time. He couldn't have been there 24 hours a day, and this person is in charge of the situation and is involved in communications. He's involved in the communications between General Mladic and those who are responsible for monitoring the task. He is a sort of mediator, in fact, a communications mediator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you told us that assistant commanders were experts in implementing orders of General Mladic. So I know that -- of course, we all know that you and others have subordinates, but are you saying that it would be General Miletic that was overall and responsible for implementing this order and monitoring it? Clearly 50 buses and them coming to Bratunac is going to take some work.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only General Miletic. All of us had our responsibilities in a certain sense. You've quite correctly understood the duties, the responsibilities I had. As for the other aspects of those duties, well, these can be -- one can see how they are carried out when monitoring the way in which the task is implemented. The logistics sector also has its security. They had to obtain and secure 10 tonnes of fuel, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you involved in the mobilisation of fuel for these buses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know who got the fuel for buses and where they got it from? The Court knows how valuable and how rare fuel was in those days.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it would be possible for you to protect me from speculation. I could try and guess who obtained or who supplied the fuel, but I don't know who did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, it's your obligation to answer the question to the best of your ability and knowledge. And, as in the past days, you should tell Mr. McCloskey everything you know. And if you don't know, you should indicate it. It's not a question of speculation. You are a well-trained army officer. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, I don't want you to speculate. Just so you know that my questions will not incorporate speculation. On the morning of the 12th, when you were able to get the paper work off to the ministry, what was your knowledge as to the purpose of those buses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the purpose of the buses was to evacuate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which people from where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know which people or from where. Or, rather, I knew that the buses were to arrive at the stadium at Bratunac at a certain time, but I didn't know which people they were to transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you didn't know the ethnic group of the people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you demobilise these buses? As the mobiliser requester, I would think that you would be the one that would do the paperwork demobilising them, sending them back.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. The Ministry of Defence has the responsibility for demobilisation because they mobilised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. When did General Mladic release those buses back so that they could get back to their normal routes and pick up people and take them to work and all the other disruptions that we saw caused by your mobilisation request? Given that you are the one following Mladic's order to mobilise, you would have, of course, known when General Mladic didn't need them anymore and to be able to tell the ministry that they were coming back, or am I wrong on that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I didn't know when it would no longer be necessary to have the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did the buses go back to the ministry? You were on duty those days.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they weren't returned to the ministry but were returned to the secretariats and municipalities that mobilised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I said "to the ministry." When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just roughly tell us how many days or weeks you have knowledge that they were used by the army for, General Mladic used them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, perhaps about ten days at the end of July. There were tasks that had to be carried out. They were essential and this was the result of the attack of the Croatian army and the ABiH in the west of Republika Srpska. So we no longer concerned ourselves with that problem. When I say "we," Your Honours, I have all the generals from the VRS Main Staff in mind and most of the officers from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first learn that the buses that you helped mobilise were used to take the women and children and old men from Potocari and Bratunac to Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the first time, but I saw video recordings of the event of that entire process. I saw such videos on the television or on a computer. Well, the Tribunal, in fact, provided such a video, and it's also possible to see these video recordings on the internet and you can then see what actually happened. Or, rather, I could see that. I am not referring to you. I do apologise. But in the Serbian language it's sometimes possible to say "we" when you mean yourself. But I saw this in this video recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When? And I don't need exact, but when it was happening, a day or two later, a week or two later?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during those days, at that time there was a video recording broadcast on television - I don't know which channel - in Han Pijesak. We could watch the Republika Srpska television. I am not sure what its name was at the time. We could also watch the Bosnia-Herzegovina television --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and again I don't know the exact name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. You've told us about your ability to watch the television. I just need to know when you found out about the movement of the population.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the Judges in this case have heard that after some 20- to 30.000 Muslim women and children or a figure somewhere around that amount were bussed and trucked out of the Bratunac and Potocari areas on the 12th and 13th. That on the morning of the 14th -- well, excuse me, on the evening of the 13th continuing on to the morning of the 13th [sic], some 5- to 6.000, at least, Muslim able-bodied men were bussed in a very large number of buses and trucks from Bratunac to an area around Zvornik. Were those the same buses and trucks that shipped the women out, or did you have to mobilise new and different buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've seen everything that concerns mobilisation and documents that have been presented at this trial, and also documents that have been presented in other cases. Fifty buses can transport 5- to 6.000 people -- well, it was necessary to mobilise other vehicles, and you were able to see that in the documents, Mr. McCloskey, that were presented by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, involved in mobilising additional vehicles for the able-bodied men that were taken to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, Mr. McCloskey. But if someone did submit a request, I wouldn't dispute the fact that that was transmitted through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Court has also heard evidence that many Muslim able-bodied men were transported all the way across Bosnia from the Srebrenica area in buses or at least a bus, if not buses, to the area of Trnovo, going across. Now, how many corps zones would you have to go across from driving from the Bratunac-Zvornik area to get to Trnovo at that time with all the various front lines? How many different corps would a bus driver have to go by or through?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is there a rule when there are more than one corps involved in a logistics situation or a battle situation that the Main Staff normally gets involved to help co-ordinate that as opposed to just letting the corps themselves do it without the Main Staff's knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's not necessarily always the case that the Main Staff would control the situation because such an action is called neighbourly co-operation. They can co-ordinate certain activities themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If it was an order from General Mladic to take Muslims from Srebrenica to Trnovo to be executed, would that be the kind of thing that the Main Staff would do the monitoring and the co-ordination of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. You have the floor. I said "Mr. Tolimir."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace upon this courtroom, and I would like this trial to be completed in according to providence, not according to my wishes. Mr. McCloskey -- it seems that Mr. McCloskey is putting to Mr. Skrbic that two corps had organised two trucks. First he asked whether they crossed the territory of the two corps and now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this question calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you. That was not the question of Mr. McCloskey. He was talking about involvement of certain units of the VRS. He was not talking about two buses in that respect. Please don't put anything in your objection to a question which could give an indication to the witness how to answer the question. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, as I think General Skrbic and I understand, we are talking about this trip from the Zvornik area across two separate VRS corps. We are not talking about 2 Corps or 2nd Corps. I don't know if that's the translation problem that it may be causing the issue, but I think General Skrbic and I know, and it was fairly evident because he named the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But in any event, general, can you answer my last question: If General Mladic had ordered busloads of Muslims be taken from the Srebrenica-Zvornik area all the way across Bosnia to the Trnovo area to be executed, would that have been monitored by his people from the Main Staff and implemented? As you say, the assistant commanders are experts in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is again a leading question. Let it be shown properly what is being presumed. I didn't say "a leading question," I said it was a question that calls for speculation, and I am kindly asking the interpreters to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is imperative for me as a questioner to have a basis of fact when I am asking him such a question, and my basis of fact - as I am sure the Court will recall - are the Srebrenica able-bodied men that were murdered in the Trnovo film in late July. You've seen that evidence. Those were Srebrenica survivors -- people that survived up until the film, according to their relatives. We've also heard from the cameraman who said that he had heard of others that he had come across, not just those six, in buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So my question is: If able-bodied men, several of them, in one or more buses, were ordered by General Mladic to be taken across Bosnia to be killed, as we saw in the film, would that have been monitored, implemented, by members of the Main Staff? And I understand the general does not want to believe such an order happened, but I have the right to ask him that in any event, even if he doesn't believe it happened. Would it have been monitored or implemented by members of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask Mr. McCloskey to tell us whether he is talking about the transportation about six soldiers in six buses or the transportation of six soldiers? The question is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am talking about six able-bodied men that we saw murdered. They came out of a truck. I don't know how they got there, but I refer him specifically - and he will recall - the testimony of the Serbian MUP videographer who said he had heard that there were others in buses or a bus. I can't remember if it was one or more. And I think we can all infer from the fact that it was more than just six people that were sent to Trnovo, especially given the evidence by the videographer. That's the basis of my question. He will recall that. That's what I am asking about. I am not making anything up here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, please answer the question of Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. What was the question? Could this question kindly be repeated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If General Mladic ordered the transport of one or more buses of able-bodied Muslim men from Srebrenica across the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to Trnovo to be executed, who or what unit in the Main Staff would have monitored and implemented that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not able to answer this question using a conditional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic and Mr. Tolimir, we have heard the last three days many questions during examination-in-chief about the structure, about responsibilities in the VRS and in the different units of the Main Staff. That was not -- that was related to the knowledge, the deep knowledge of one of the six assistant commanders. During cross-examination it is absolutely acceptable to put these kind of questions to a witness. So, Mr. Skrbic, if we take away the condition Mr. McCloskey put to you, who would be responsible for monitoring the transport of people, be it prisoners of war or others, from one area of responsibility of a corps to another area of another corps? Who would be responsible to monitor such a movement in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that would be units of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, does the security organ of the brigades of the corps and of the Main Staff have a professional responsibility over the actions and use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, professional responsibility. But in terms of command, no, because it has been stipulated by a singleness of command and subordination. I said, Your Honours, that members of the MUP as well, but since no state of war was declared at the time, it is possible that they were involved in this escort in a co-ordinated action, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, general. We understand that the MPs have their own commanders and they are commanded by their brigade commanders or their corps commanders or their Main Staff commanders, and the question had to do with General Mladic's issuing the command, and you've told us that it would be the military police involved. And now you have agreed that it would be the security organs that oversee the professional management of the military police. So it wouldn't be General Mladic managing the movement of these prisoners, it would be the military police and the security organs that manage them professionally. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let's avoid hypothetical questions. Can Mr. McCloskey give us any specifics concerning General Mladic's order and confirm whether any such order existed at all? So let us not force the witness to give answers based on assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I already explained the witness is here to testify as that was -- as your witness to testify about the internal structure and the chain of command in the Main Staff and in the VRS. So you put questions of that kind to the witness and Mr. McCloskey is entitled to do the same during his cross-examination. Sir, please answer the last question of Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the affairs of the military police and the organs of the security are not identical. Security organ from General Staff all to the brigade provide security of the facilities, whereas the military police is involved in combat and police work. Therefore, my answer is that these two kinds of jobs cannot intermingle. Why would security organs monitor the passage of any convoy whatsoever unless they suspected there might be some suspicious element within the convoy that might lead to sabotage actions or alike? The military police and the security organs did not discharge identical duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel Ljubisa Beara was the chief of security in the Main Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of security administration was Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the Drina Corps it was Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security chief at the command of the corps was Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware that from the 14th and the 15th and the 16th of July, that both Colonel Beara and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic were working very closely with the military police in the transport of the able-bodied men to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can leave that subject. Though, let me ask you one question related to General Tolimir's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you come to that, there is one thing unclear for me. I just wanted to clarify that with the witness. Mr. Skrbic, you were asked, and this was my question: "Who would be responsible to monitor such a movement in the Main Staff?" Your answer was: "That would be units of the military police." Were the units of the military police part of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they were part of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and this regiment was a staff unit of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, a staff unit of the Army of Republika Srpska? A unit of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was responsible in the Main Staff to monitor the actions of this regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the protection regiment, Colonel Milomir Savcic. He was directly subordinate to the commander of the VRS Main Staff. As for professional part of work involving training, deployment, and training of security organs was under the auspices of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've heard here that the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, which had their base in Nova Kasaba, was responsible for hundreds and hundreds of prisoners on 13 July, and their commander, Mr. Malinic, met with Colonel Beara who was - as you've just told us - the chief of the security of the Main Staff. Now, we've also heard from Mr. Keserovic. What was his job in the Main Staff related to military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the duty of Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was charged with professional supervision of the military police. Not only in the 65th Protection Regiment but all across the entire structure of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P02226.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general -- well, this is another line-and-block chart. The last one you saw with was used with Mr. Obradovic from the Main Staff. This one was more complete. We asked more questions. I believe this was General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we zero-in on the section for rear services, which is right there in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we know, that's General Djukic's sector. And I know this is not very satisfactory, but we can see at the bottom there is a -- one of the many separate units. It's called the transport service. And we see a Lieutenant-Colonel Kerkez, Zeljko, in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that can be just blown up. Just that section in each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this, as far as you know, the correct diagram or the -- was there a transport service in the rear -- the rear services section that was led by Lieutenant-Colonel Kerkez?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accuracy of the translation cannot be said to be in the spirit of the Serbian language. It was translated as "transportation service," whereas it should be "transport service." Anyway, this is not in dispute. As for everything else that you said, Mr. McCloskey is correct. The head of the transportation service in the logistics was, indeed, the person whose name is entered here and his rank is also correct. Later on he became a colonel, but that is irrelevant at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did -- as far as your recollection, was Colonel Kerkez or his unit involved with these -- any of these buses or transportation issues associated with the buses that you made the mobilisation request for, Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was their duty to supply fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did his unit do regarding this transportation of the Muslims and the buses and the fuel, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no more than two or three persons in that transportation service, and I don't know what they did exactly, Mr. McCloskey. I suppose that they co-ordinated all these activities over the phone or whatever. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am not asking for exacts and I don't want you to speculate. Just tell us what you do know or you can reasonably infer. That's fine, too. That's what -- General Tolimir was relying on your knowledge and your ability to infer from his questions. I don't want you to speculate. Supposing doesn't help. What did you know that this unit and these guys were doing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from roads and co-operation with the civilian traffic police, I know for sure that one of their responsibilities was to supply fuel. And since we are talking about buses, I presume that it was diesel fuel. As for the other aspect of their scope of responsibility, that is something that I don't know about. Your Honours, if I know and I am knowledgeable about the structure of the army, its organisation and everything else, that's fine, but nobody can have full knowledge about what every organ is supposed to do. So if I receive a request to provide such information about any specific organ, I comply. Now, I would like to add that my specialty is air force and missile units. Even if you ask me about my area of expertise, I couldn't maybe give you always an answer because people tend to forget. But to ask me what each individual did, this is way too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, there is no problem with that. This is the situation for every witness. But you have to tell everything you know. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 2738.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, this should be another one of those intercepts, like the one that General Tolimir showed you between a Krsmanovic and a Toso, but this one is -- that one was on 16 July, this one is on 12 July, the day we know that you sent your written request. And we can see from this that it's at 1425 hours, between a Lieutenant-Colonel Kerkez. And we have the translation "traffic," and he's identified as K, and an unidentified male, X. And he identifies himself over the air and is speaking about a few trailer trucks needed to engage in the direction down towards Bratunac. And X is -- they are talking about these vehicles leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this document should not be broadcast. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Kerkez says: "Two buses report to you from the Eastern Bosnia Corps command," he gives the registration plates. "Have them tanked up a bit ..." And so this is just -- in your view, does this have to do with the buses going to Bratunac on the 12th, the same thing you sent your mobilisation request out for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a connection, Mr. McCloskey. Only I presume -- sorry, if I am too close to the mike, but I have to look at the document. Only I assume that these buses had already been mobilised in Bijeljina because I see they have civilian license plates. Let me draw your attention to K entry where you have BN 110-147 and BN 110-20. These are civilian license plates, whereas the army had designations VRS. But yes, you're right. There is a connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your previous answer to me then would be correct because you did say he was involved in this process and he's -- with fuel, and he's at least saying tank up that one vehicle. So that would leave us to believe that you were correct in your answer regarding that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the point of view of fuel supply, as I explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I just wanted to inquire whether this document is really under seal. If not, there is no need to redact anything. Please clarify, because I can't find it in your list of documents to be used with this witness. Please help me with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be on my list. We did send a few lists over as we were collecting, so you may not have a recent one. But we cannot find any initials or any problems on it, so I don't think there is a problem it being public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then there is no problem with broadcasting it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- and I would offer that 65 ter 2738 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go back -- oops.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2738 shall be assigned Exhibit P2863. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go back to Exhibit P2656.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the 16 July intercept that the general told you about that you spoke of for a while with him. Now, did you know a Krsmanovic in the transport or traffic unit of the Drina Corps or know of him? We know personnel guys may not know everybody, but they certainly see a lot of names and promotions and such.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, at the time I knew two individuals whose surname was Krsmanovic. There was Aleksa Krsmanovic, assistant commander in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps for logistics, and I also knew another Krsmanovic whose name I cannot remember. At the time he was the Chief of Staff in the 2nd Romanija Brigade. At the time I didn't know any Krsmanovic's from the Drina Corps. I don't exclude the possibility that there was a Krsmanovic in that corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 7599. That is a new 65 ter number, Mr. President, that I -- we've identified this in our responding to the questions of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, any objection to add this document to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no objections to anything that might help to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, leave is granted to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, it -- this looks like a personnel-type document. As we see, it's from the commander of the Drina Corps, dated the 1st of October, 1995, Radislav Krstic. And it has a person named Rajko Krsmanovic, chief of the traffic and transport service in the rear service organ of the Drina Corps and a colonel. I am surprised you wouldn't know a colonel in the Drina Corps right next to you in Han Pijesak. Does this help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's a lieutenant-colonel, not a colonel. And he wasn't with me in Han Pijesak, but you can see it's Rajko here. There are two Krsmanovics. There is Rajko and the Chief of Staff in the 2nd Romanija Corps for a certain period of time, but here's the proof. Why didn't you show me this immediately so that I could tell you that it's a personal [as interpreted] document that concerns deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is from General Krstic. This should have hit your desk. Perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me just have a look at the document. Everything is a bit muddled here, and it's not addressed to anyone. Why would it be on my desk?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I get some help, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of the Court Usher a hard copy should be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't need to get into -- could he -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First to Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we don't need to get into whether this would be your desk or not. Perhaps a recommendation like that this wouldn't get to your desk. I just want to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give it to Mr. Tolimir. Please give it to Mr. Tolimir. Wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's on the screen, so I'm not -- it's not an original. I mean, it's fine, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's let Mr. Tolimir look at it, the first page of it, of course. Only that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now please give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, please take your time to look at it and the second page as well, and whether it's on your desk is not and really not an issue, and I don't mean to suggest it is. So just take your time to look at it a bit, and why I asked you the question first is because I would ideally like your recollections as opposed to you just repeating what you see on documents. So that's kind of normal in a trial. So have you had a chance to look at it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, even before I was given the document, I wanted to apologise. So please accept my apology. I didn't see the last sentence which quite explicitly says that it was on my desk, because it's a proposal for a promotion. Your Honours, under the word "healthy" it says: "Fulfills the conditions stipulated by law for promotion ..." And I immediately drew the conclusion that that had to be in the sector where I worked with Colonel Malcic in the personnel domain, so that's why I apologise, Mr. McCloskey. I didn't have time to have a look at the whole document. And there is an explanation about this proposal from the corps commander, this proposal for promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And here is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it this is attached to the hard copy the witness has in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. And we see that -- I think we should see that they are -- they should be sequential ERN numbers, meaning they were stamped from one to the other, which indicates that when we got them they were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what we see here, and I won't go over all of it in detail, is a discussion about his history and the good job he was doing. And then as we get down to the seventh paragraph -- it's actually the third from the bottom. It says: "He put a lot of effort and with great success organised and transported Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa." So with this personnel document that you say should have gone -- or did go on your desk because you've already told us the Main Staff had to approve these kind of promotions, and that you can see he was a Drina Corps guy. He was involved, according to General Krstic, with the same kind of buses and stuff that Kerkez was that you just talked about in the same unit, one -- Main Staff, Kerkez. Krsmanovic, the corps. Does this help refresh your recollection as to your knowledge of this man, either his existence as a personnel guy that you didn't know or someone that you actually now remember you knew because you might have had contact with him? Vlasenica and Han Pijesak being very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't meet the gentleman until 1995, when he became the commander of a brigade in Romanija. Or, rather, it was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you do now. This helps you remember this person. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we briefly go to 65 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I would offer that document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7599 shall be assigned Exhibit P2864. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to 65 ter 7597.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a -- a listing of the people on the Drina Corps on April 29th, 1995, which includes Veljko Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would ask leave for this because it's on the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am sure that Mr. Tolimir has no objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list. As he generally told us that he has no objection to this kind of application. Please continue. Leave is granted to do that this. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document, general, that we received from the Drina Corps collection that we have. And is this the same Veljko Krsmanovic we just saw being recommended for promotion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have to be precise about something. Mr. McCloskey is using the name "Veljko" but here it says "Rajko." Mr. McCloskey, could you please repeat your question, who do you have in mind, Veljko or Rajko?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, thank you for correcting me. Rajko, son of Veljko Krsmanovic, who was the person on the promotion recommendation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Rajko Krsmanovic, son of Veljko, is on the list, and that is the individual concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7597 shall be assigned Exhibit P2865. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P1539. Sorry, 1539C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this will be an intercept from 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the middle one, general, that starts at 0922 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this one should not be broadcast. Yeah. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It does have the name of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yeah, it should not be broadcast. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Taking some time with the English, but I don't need to spend too much time with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As, again, we see a Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic, unidentified person. And X tells him that they only have two buses, some other can be mobilised without papers, without an order. But they have a problem with fuel. They don't have enough of it. How would they be able to get buses without mobilising them? What would the options be? I ...

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From their own unit's sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, P156 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you please tell us, is this document under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am told it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is not -- there is no indication that it is under seal in your exhibit list. That's the reason why I am asking it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was told that it was only marked for identification. I don't know the reason at the moment. Are you tendering it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It had a P number, P1539C, so I didn't think we got P number -- but I offer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are quite a lot of documents marked for identification with a P or a D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We best offer that, I'm sorry. I should know by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After some years. It will be received now under this document number. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could we now go to P1563, and I believe it should be confidential as well. And it's C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, the one I'd like you to look at in the B/C/S is the one that's at 1200 hours on 12 July. It's that first one between X and Y. And it just is a lot of information about 25 buses, various places, three from some place they are not sure, five from some place they are not sure, nine buses from Pale and Sokolac, one tractor trailer from Bratunac, three tractor trailers from -- is that Batkovici or Bratkovici? I see it's Bratkovici, okay. And Radakovic is asking permission to use 14 trucks. He will keep them in reserve. They talk about the 35th base in Bijeljina. Some more that I won't mention. And a request for fuel has been sent to Krstic. Now, if this is General Krstic, would this, in your view, be related to the mobilisation or the -- if not mobilisation, the gathering together of buses from all over to deal with the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comme ci, comme ca. That's how I would put it. Yes, this is a process that was initiated in relation to mobilisation. So the buses had set off and it was necessary to obtain fuel for them and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And are you familiar with an auto battalion in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this battalion was a part of the Drina Corps as per establishment, that auto battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know a Radakovic in that unit or had you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've probably heard of him, but I didn't know him, Mr. McCloskey. It is a battalion, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, had you heard of him or not? You said "probably," or that's ...

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "probably" because he was in our personnel files, if he was an officer. Since he was a battalion commander he was probably an officer. I don't know whether he was a reserve officer or an active-duty officer. If he was a professional officer, then he was in the personnel files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But prior to that, I just want to take us back to, briefly, P2656. The intercept that you spent some time on with General Tolimir. And I just want us to look at it. It is from 16th July, as we know from the record, at 2143 hours, between Krsmanovic and Toso. And it says in a discussion with Toso about the problem with transportation, Krsmanovic mentioned 10 buses and 14 trucks in relation to the means that are not yet requisitioned. And in quotes: "That was the situation today." So we can see here these two people are having a discussion about problems with buses and trucks on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now let's go to 65 ter 2748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can remember, in the course of my testimony I said that this was not -- please, could we go back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is conducting his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, general, did you want to explain something about one of your answers to General Tolimir? Because I haven't really asked you anything yet on that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I apologise, Mr. McCloskey. There is just something I wanted to add that's all. You said that this was a conversation, but I said - I don't know if I am right - that it wasn't a conversation. It says Krsmanovic, and then it quotes what Krsmanovic said. That is the only distinction I wanted to make, Your Honours. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The English translation we have is: "In a discussion with Toso ..." So I don't know how you're getting that, but conversation or discussion, these in English are similar words. In any event, let's now -- and we see this intercept, which is a little over two hours earlier at 1859 hours between a Krsmanovic and Goran. It's between Krsmanovic and someone named Goran. And Krsmanovic asked Goran to take two buses back to him, which he did prior to this. And Krsmanovic continues. And now it says: "I also sent Golic and his ten," and that's just -- we don't know a ten what, "back yesterday ... I was granted these ten upon Kerkez's decision ... is it still ... does Kerkez know if this is still on?" Goran says: "What do you mean, you still need it? Why?" Kerkez says: "I need them to transport people. Today, my superior officer demanded that he should go immediately to the region to transport ... because the action is not completed." Goran says: "Do you have the remaining 20 --"

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't follow you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's break time so I think if we can -- I can give a hard copy to read, though, if you want to do that on your break, otherwise we will start at the end of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. We all haven't seen this yet. If I am correct, this document is under seal and we will see how to proceed. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, please take your earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we were at that intercept, 65 ter 2748. And I just want to see if we can identify possible parties in this. And to remind us, this is an intercept that is about two and three-quarter hours before the intercept about the discussion between Krsmanovic and Toso and the problem with ten buses. So we see that -- and I won't read it all, but just starting from the beginning Krsmanovic is asking someone by the name of Goran to take two buses back to him. And then Krsmanovic says: "I also sent Golic and his ten back yesterday ... I was granted these ten upon Kerkez's decision ..." And it goes on. Do you know a -- and we know that Golic is a common name, but do you know a Major -- did you know a Major Golic in the intel section of the Drina Corps, Pavle Golic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. But I didn't know that he was in the intelligence. I knew a Golic who was a communication chief at the corps command for a certain period of time. I cannot remember. He may have been transferred to the intelligence section, that same Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then Krsmanovic says: "I need them to transport people. Today my superior officer demanded that he should go immediately to the region to transport ... because the action is not finished." So if Krsmanovic is an officer in the Drina Corps, who was the commander of the Drina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you please remind me of the date of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it's 16 July.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Radislav Krstic was already the corps commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on the 16th of July, did you know that General Krstic was engaged in the -- commanding the operation into the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it goes on. Goran says: "Do you have the remaining 20 or something that is not from the auto battalion from your region?" We've already talked about the Drina Corps's auto battalion in Zvornik. Krsmanovic says: "Do you hear what I am asking you, man?" And then he says: "Is Kerkez around somewhere?" And Goran says he's having dinner. And then Krsmanovic says: "Tell him I was looking for him and that I will call him in a while. I am trying to tell you something and you --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... and you ... fuck it, you are telling your story." Goran says: "And you are telling yours." Now, if Krsmanovic is asking a guy named Goran about Kerkez and Goran knows that Kerkez is at dinner, were you aware of any subordinate of Kerkez named Goran? Would have been at the Main Staff because, as you've told us, Kerkez is the Main Staff guy for transport. I think you've told us Djukic is in Han Pijesak with you, so I would think Djukic's guys are in the same Han Pijesak admin building with you, not up at Crna Rijeka, but you know better than I.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. It's right. They were in Han Pijesak, not in Crna Rijeka. Now, back to your question. I cannot agree with you with any degree of certainty that K stands for Krsmanovic, that G stands for Golic and so on. I can see the letter K and then the letter G, then again the letter K and so on and so forth. If someone has identified these individuals for you, I have no problem with that. But I, myself, cannot say that I know who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, the question was: "... were you aware of any subordinate of Kerkez named Goran?" Please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, we have heard from several intercept operators that did these, and just so you know, when I ask you the question I -- the -- they have told us that the -- Krsmanovic would be K and G would be Goran because that's how they did it. They would put it up on the top and then it would go on like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would like to offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2748 shall be assigned Exhibit P2866.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now could we go to D341.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is that list that General Tolimir gave you. It was your Main Staff list that had all the people in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This would be page 19 of that list. It's the one the general wanted to have complete -- we are now translating the complete one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it should be the traffic and transportation service under 103 and then 4300.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so if we could blow that one up. It's 103 4300. It says -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see up there Zeljko Kerkez. What's his job?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, up there you can see the title: "Transportation and Traffic Service," and underneath it says, "Chief." First Ostoja Stijepic, son of Novak, was before Mr. Zeljko Kerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, so who was the chief in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Kerkez was the chief in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go down to the referents. These men would have been stationed at the Han Pijesak administrative building where you were, where you would have spent a lot of your time. And we see one of those referents is named Goran. Did you know a Goran that worked -- I will ask the same question, does this help refresh your recollection of a man that worked in the same building as you did and worked for Kerkez named Goran Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Now I remember who Goran was. Now that you told me that his last name was Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The English is in e-court but I think that should be clear enough for everyone and it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, just another topic I want to switch to, and hopefully briefly. General Tolimir asked you on page 18636 about the resubordination by the police to the army. And you answered, and I quote: "According to what I know, there was no resubordination whatsoever." And then you say that the police are resubordinated to the army only during a state of war and no specific document has been issued to that effect because they become an integral part of the armed forces. Because a state of war wasn't proclaimed in the territory of Republika Srpska until the 20th of October, 1995. Though I think somewhere else in your testimony you said that they did declare a state of war about -- around Srebrenica in July. So I won't hold you to that October. Do you remember when you talked about a state of war in Srebrenica in July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, Mr. McCloskey. It was around July. And I think you do have documents on the proclamation of a state of war, as well as the order signed by the president of the republic. I believe I've seen these documents somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I'll -- if I have time I may show that to you. And you recall you and I discussed this topic in your interview, and I believe I showed you some documents on it, this resubordination issue, but perhaps we can just get right to the point. I -- let's not use this term "resubordination." Let me just simplify it. Were you aware that special police forces, in this case commanded by the deputy commander of the special police force unit that was under the Ministry of the Interior, were actually sent to Srebrenica and put under the command of General Mladic on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I did not dispute the documents showed me by you in 2005, but up to that time I hadn't known that they were sent there. Now I can only confirm the information contained in these documents that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you told General Krstic for whatever reason he elicited from you, and I quote -- sorry, from General Tolimir: "According to what I know, there was no resubordination whatsoever." And as you know resubordination puts a unit in the command of another.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. McCloskey. I have no reason to go back on what I said, and I would like to repeat that I began my answer with the words "According to what I know ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P2516. We will just go through some of these documents that I showed you before because we'll see if that fits to what you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that this is dated 10 July. It's in the name of the staff commander who is from the Ministry of the Interior, Tomislav Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version be enlarged further, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see it's directed to a number of police forces. And it makes reference to: "Pursuant to the order of the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska armed forces," and that's Radovan Karadzic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And: "In order to crush the enemy offensive being carried out from the safe area of Srebrenica I hereby order ..." And I don't want to go through the details of it, but we can see, as I said, that it designated, in number 3, Ljubisa Borovcanin to be the commander of these units. And then if we go down to point 5, it says: "On arrival at his destination, the unit commander is obliged to make contact with the corps Chief of Staff, General Krstic." So if this means Borovcanin is to make contact with General Krstic, what does that mean, if anything, to you regarding who is in command of who or working with who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I understand this to mean that they were co-operating with each other, although I cannot definitely say who commanded whom. They were both commanders. They had to talk to each other. They had to agree on further actions pursuant to the orders received from the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think deputy commander, which is roughly equivalent to colonel, Borovcanin -- that General Mladic had to agree with this -- with Borovcanin, this colonel, before Borovcanin could be acted upon?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why you have mentioned General Mladic. We are talking about General Krstic and Mr. Borovcanin. I don't know whether he had any rank or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the same thing holds for General Krstic. Do you think General Krstic couldn't order Borovcanin after he reported to him that he would have to agree and sort of work together in some sort co-operative way in a military combat situation? Please, general, give us your best military opinion on this.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, at the time to which this document refers, which was not sent to the Drina Corps command, you see on the top who the recipient was, they were still within the relationship that involved co-operation. What happened afterwards, I don't know. I do not rule out the possibility that General Krstic, as the Drina Corps commander, and given that this unit was sent to him, he might have become their commander as well. I don't exclude that as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to P1335. This is Mr. Borovcanin's after-action report of the events from the -- about the 10th of July through about the 20th of July, and it should be looking at the first page of the English there. Let's get you up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see in the English that he does mention the order that we just looked at from on 10 July where he was sent to participate in the Srebrenica operation. And then in the English he talks about his travelling from the 10th and the 11th in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need to go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S you can find the part. The paragraph says: "When we arrived in Bratunac at 1200 hours on 11 July, we acquainted ourselves with the situation on the front, where intense fighting was taking place at the very entrance to Srebrenica town from the direction of Pribicevac and Zeleni Jadar. "From the observer post in Pribicevac, I contacted General Mladic, who personally commanded over the operation. On receipt of combat papers, he ordered me to that same day with all available manpower and equipment from the direction of Zuti Most to Potocari ..." and onward. Does that clear up this issue for you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Only obviously this date was added by someone. I don't know who. Added by hand, 11th of July, by 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you now agree with me that Borovcanin and his MUP forces are now under the command of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was no way for them not to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go to another part of this, where on page 18618 you began speaking to General Tolimir about can -- and he said to you: "Can you remember any general that was retired in mid-July 1995?" And you said: "Yes, that was Milenko Zivanovic." And you said you ... I'm sorry, let me just make sure we get this clear. On the bottom of that page, the general says: "Thank you. Do you remember when he retired and who was responsible for the paperwork for his retirement?" And you said: "The decree that I took to the president of the republic was signed by the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, on the 14th of July, 1995. The decree defined specifically the date of the retirement, and I believe that was on the same day; in other words, as of 14 July 1995 he was retired." Did anyone from the Defence show you those documents at this -- before this hearing? I think you've probably seen them before. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, no one from the Defence showed me that document, that I created it, then it was signed. So if I saw it, then I would confirm those dates, but I think the dates are correct. But I don't remember whether it says that he retired on the 14th, but it is usual -- it's part of military practice for the date when it's signed meaning that -- the date when the document was signed would show when the actual person retired. If we could see the document, it would be easier to say. I think that decree exists, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we -- I want to get to it. But first I want to just show you something. I mean, you said it was the 14th July that you saw President Karadzic. What do you base that on? Is it just your memory or where you had a chance to see a diary or anything?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in Belgrade I, in fact, told you that I made certain notes on my computer and these notes were made from memory. And it is on that basis that I drew the conclusion that I must have been there on the 14th or around that date because of that decree that concerned the retirement of General Zivanovic and the appointment of certain other generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What other generals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appointment of General Krstic as the commander of the Drina Corps, and the appointment of Colonel Svetozar Andric as the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. So only one general was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have P2198. It should be e-court page 79, B/C/S e-court page 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this should be, if I got my numbers right, a diary that the secretaries of President Karadzic put together and told us about. And we should be seeing the entry for 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we go to e-court page 91. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see it's an appointment diary. Familiar name of Miroslav Deronjic. It's before you. And then we see General Skrbic, 1215 hours to 1235 hours. So you got 20 minutes. Does that seem about right? Or does it help you at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the secretary told us that if they put a plus by the person's name, that meant that it actually occurred, that meeting. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 811.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, we see that this is a decree from the president of the Republika Srpska. It's signed in the name of Radovan Karadzic. And it talks about placed at the disposal of the Main Staff Milenko Zivanovic. Is this the decree that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It doesn't say "retired," but can you just tell us what that means, "placed at the disposal," in this context?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. If the Main Staff has the need, they then retain him and make a proposal to the president for a certain appointment. This is again done by a decree. If there is no such need, then his employment is terminated. The Main Staff didn't have the need for Milenko Zivanovic, General Milenko Zivanovic, and as a result he ceased to be fully employed. He was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see a stamp over President Karadzic's signature. And we also have a stamp on the original with the name Radoslav Banduka. Is that the same Banduka that you spoke of the other day when writing in that little box in a chart of the Main Staff? Can you remind us who that is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, that's correct. That's the individual from the Ministry of Defence who was, as far as I can remember, acting as an assistant to Mr. Kovacevic. I don't know his exact position, but he was in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this isn't Rajko Banduka, Mladic's guy?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you type this up? You said you typed up the paperwork at the Main Staff and brought it over, when you were telling that to General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't do that myself, Mr. McCloskey. It was done in our department. A draft was made on the computer. These letters are letters I can't really recognise, but within the Ministry of Defence, this must have been typed out again and then taken to the president. I don't remember which document I took to the president, whether it was this one or the other one that we compiled. I don't know which document I took to the president for him to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Because we see here this is 15 July, and from your memory and from the appointments book, you were there on the 14th of July. Can you account for why it's a 15 July date that he's signing off on this? Would you have typed it up the day before -- sorry, the day after for him to sign?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you've seen in the previous documents that I was at the president's on the 14th. That is quite certain. Now, I cannot remember this exactly, but given these documents perhaps it wasn't signed at the very same time. But I took that decree to the ministry for them to have a look at and then they signed it on the 15th. That might be a reasonable explanation for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we can offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter document 811 shall be assigned Exhibit P2867. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to 65 ter 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, you'll see as this one comes up it's another decree. It's the same type, same Radovan Karadzic stamp signature. This one has to do with the -- appointing General Krstic as commander, which you've just told us about. And this -- this is -- has got a spot where you handwrite -- somebody handwrites in the date and this is 14 July. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is a document from the sector I worked in, and this is what documents looked like when I worked on the computer. This was in the sector of the Main Staff of the department for mobilisation, organisation, et cetera. And this document was signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. So, I wasn't quite sure which document he had signed and hadn't signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, in direct examination you remembered going to see Karadzic about the retirement of Zivanovic and now you've been able to recall that not only it had to do with the retirement of Zivanovic but also the promotion to General Krstic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. But I haven't remembered it now. I knew it then. You didn't ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, General Tolimir didn't ask you about Krstic and you were able to remember it. So that's -- I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to offer that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 18 shall be assigned Exhibit P2868. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we've now established that you would have spoken to him briefly at some point in that 20 minutes about the retirement of Zivanovic and the promotion to General Krstic. And two days prior to that, you had sent his ministry a request for buses that his ministry acted upon, as we saw. And just to put you in bit of context, on the 14th of July -- excuse me, on the evening of the 13th of July, all the women and children and old men had been shipped out by many buses and trucks out of Potocari and are now in Muslim-held territory. But on the night of the 13th, there are thousands and thousands of Muslim able-bodied men in Bratunac and in the area and schools. And this Court has heard evidence that President Karadzic that evening had a conversation with Miroslav Deronjic, who met with him right before you did on the 14th, about moving parcels out of the Bratunac area. So my question is: When you see the president on the 14th at about noon at which time thousands of men are being transported from Bratunac to Zvornik in a column led by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, did you discuss or did Radovan Karadzic mention any of those details, the buses needed for the transport of all those men, or anything to do with that topic?
