That now, by the 14th of July, is being commanded by General Krstic from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. McCloskey, that wasn't discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say, "as far as I can remember" -- oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps Mr. McCloskey should indicate the time when Deronjic and Karadzic met, because it was stated on the document that we had a look at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a proposal for Mr. McCloskey. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I had -- I think I had said that right before the general's meeting with President Karadzic that Miroslav Deronjic had met with him. And if we go back to that exhibit, we see that General Skrbic was 1215 to 1235, and Deronjic's was actually 1240 to 1310 hours. It was originally scheduled at 1100 hours. So it was actually after his meeting. So thank you for correcting me on that. Precision is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So you had your questions said -- sorry, in your answer to me, "As far as I can remember, that wasn't discussed." That's the same thing you said to me when I asked you if Srebrenica had been mentioned at Zivanovic's going-away party. So, general, please, can you get back into your memory and give us your best memory. Anything to do with the Srebrenica events. It was a historical event, after all.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I can't remember the things you would like me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. One other personnel document on a related topic. Do you know when General Mladic actually made General Krstic the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you please put the question to me again? Because General Mladic didn't have the responsibility for appointing officers who had the rank of a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was General Krstic actually made commander of the Drina Corps by whoever?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1995, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I take it -- what do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base it on the president's decree that you showed to me a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But as the personnel man, you would know the -- some of the backdrop and background into how it was that a person gets retired right between major actions, Srebrenica and then Zepa? And how it would occur at such a volatile and complex time that one becomes a commander and one is retired. So do you recall any other circumstances, aside from this one document? Was this a planned event? I mean, most generals' promotions are known pretty far in advance as well as retirements. Or was he -- was Zivanovic retired suddenly without your knowledge? Can you give us a little background. I don't want to go in -- I know personnel issues can get pretty complex. I don't want to know that. But basically, what else besides this document are you basing your testimony on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Just a few facts I would like to inform you of. General Zivanovic was wounded. I think that was back in 1993. Or I don't know the exact year. I remember that at a collegium, at a meeting, on one occasion there was a discussion about who should be the chief of the staff of the Drina Corps, whether it should be Colonel Krstic. He was a colonel at the time, that was in mid-1994. It was also discussed whether it should be Colonel Skocajic Milutin. We then suggested to the commander that Colonel Radislav Krstic should occupy that position. As far as the proposal for appointing General Krstic as commander and also to retire General Zivanovic, this wasn't discussed at the collegium as is customary. General Mladic acted within his purview, and he suggested to the president of the republic, to Mr. Karadzic, that Zivanovic should be retired and that the commander of the Drina Corps should be General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P2357.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's see if this may help refresh your recollection as to the dates and the specifics of this transfer. And you'll have a chance to study that, but can you first tell us: Have you ever heard of anyone named -- chief of personnel and legal affairs of the Drina Corps, Lieutenant-Colonel Radenko Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I have, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you study this personnel document from Jovicic? We see it's dated 13 July and it was received by a unit at 2325 hours on the 13th of July according to that stamp at the bottom. And it's pretty self-explanatory, transfer of duties of the corps commander. And it says: "Pursuant to the decree of the president of Republika Srpska, and in the presence of the VRS Main Staff commander, Colonel General Ratko Mladic, the transfer of duties of the Drina Corps commander duties was carried out on 13 July 1995." And it talks about Mladic -- excuse me, Krstic getting the job and Andric getting the Chief of Staff job. And of course it says: "Acquaint all members of your unit in the appropriate manner with this document."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor kindly repeat his last question, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says -- I am getting at the point where I don't remember what I just said. But I was just reiterating what the document was saying, "Acquaint all members of your unit in the appropriate manner regarding this document."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber and the interpreters were waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall -- what's going on here? This is the 13th of July. You just said the 14th. Does this help refresh your recollection of what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I think that this is a rational explanation. Let me draw your attention to the beginning of the sentence, "On the basis of a decree by the president of Republika Srpska," but where is the number of the decree? Why didn't this personnel officer write down the number? So they were expecting a decree on appointment, but the transfer of duties had already been carried out and I don't dispute that. Although I don't know when this was done, but in the document you can see that it was on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, President Karadzic and General Mladic could have agreed to the promotion on the 13th, and President Karadzic said, "I do decree and I will get the paperwork to you," and General Mladic could have gone on and done it right there on the 13th. Is that one way it could have happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right, Mr. McCloskey. That was a possible scenario. It wouldn't have been possible to do things differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard the account that General Mladic on his way back from the Bratunac area on the early evening of 13 July with some of his people stopped at the Vlasenica command of the Drina Corps, lined up the assembled officers who were there - Krstic, Zivanovic - and said something to the effect of, "General Krstic, you are now in command. General Zivanovic, you are retired." Have you heard that accounting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard that, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, let's go to 65 ter 677. This should be the "Decision on the Proclamation of a State of War in Srebrenica, Skelani Municipality." It has a date of 14 July 1995 on it. Is this what you were referring to when you were talking about the state of war, the declaration there -- or the proclamation in the Srebrenica municipality earlier?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your office or the Main Staff have anything to do with the drafting of this or would this have been drafted at the president's office?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, our service didn't have anything to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we can see that obviously this is 14 July, it's the Srebrenica/Skelani area. We all know what events had taken place and are taking place in that area, which roughly starts around Cerska all the way down past Skelani. What -- what input did the -- anybody from the VRS have in -- in this -- in this proclamation? Any discussions with the army beforehand by the president? Did the president do this on his own, as far as you know? What do you know about this, since it certainly appears - as we look at it - it has a lot to do with the army's ability to obtain men and materiel without mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I know that we from the military constantly recommended to the president to proclaim the state of war from 1992 onwards until the end of the war. The president ignored our requests. Therefore, we did not know that a state of war would be declared in the Srebrenica area, and when I say "we," I mean the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is an indication of -- you finally succeeded in convincing the president to do this. Who -- who succeeded? Was it Mladic, was it Milovanovic, was it General Tolimir? Who has the success on his belt, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody was consulted with regard to this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the president did this on his own. We were all surprised when a state of war was declared only in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you with the other assistant commanders on the 14th of July where they were all surprised? Is that how you know that none of them had any role in any of this? You actually did go to one of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Mr. McCloskey, whether we learned about this decision immediately on the 14th of July. As far as my sector is concerned, we discussed this much later after we had heard of it. The war was in full sway, and then a state of war was declared only in the area of Srebrenica. Wouldn't you, yourself, find it odd?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I asked you because not but two days before you had to go through this process of mobilising a request through Karadzic's ministry. On the 14th of July this is happening, their buses are coming, people are being transported. This has direct consequences - does it not? - on the your work, the work of Kerkez down the hall in the Main Staff, the other assistant commanders on other various levels. This is something you would have found out immediately, if not before; correct? Now that you have had a chance to think about, general, don't you think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, he is always waiting for the finalising of the interpretation. Now your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if the question was clear. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mobilisation is a process that lasts throughout a war. In response to Mr. Tolimir's question, I explained what kind of mobilisation is effected during a wartime and what kind of mobilisation we have in other situations. Therefore, I don't deny that we in the sector were aware of the pending mobilisation, that it was potentially going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you mean you were aware of the pending proclamation of state of war before it happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, but just to help us get a little bit of an understanding of it, we -- we see it's for a particular area, Srebrenica, Skelani. Paragraph 3 talks about: "The armed forces in the zone of Drina Corps shall take all necessary measures to accomplish the set goals by the organised and effective use of available resources." And then it goes on and says: "In compliance with its constitutional and legal powers, the government, ministries, and all other state organs in the republic are obliged to fully implement the decision on general mobilisation and provide the armed forces with the necessary human and material conditions for the successful conduct of the war." So this proclamation basically makes the civilian structures, as mentioned here, they have to provide you with what you need to wage war. Is that the bottom line? In this area.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to where we are on the 14th of July, the women and children are no longer in Srebrenica. There is no old men, either. And by the morning of the 14th of July, all the prisoners, the thousands of prisoners have been shipped up to Zvornik which is not in the Srebrenica/Skelani area, but there are still hundreds of Muslim men in the woods probably north of Potocari, Susnjari, Jaglici, and around Cerska. So what's the big mobilisation of men and materials for Srebrenica for, as far as you know? Zepa has just started, the attack on Zepa has just started the morning of the 14th. Tolimir is down there. He needs men and material as well. So what's this for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no justified requirements. All the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness please rephrase the answer. The interpreters couldn't understand him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will try to simplify it. With most of action in Eastern Bosnia not being in Srebrenica and Skelani anymore, it's in Zvornik and in Zepa, with hundreds of men running around the woods in the north part of the enclave, what's the need to mobilise men and materiel in the Srebrenica area? You're the mobilisation guy. You're at your desk. You know about this. Just give us your best memory. What is needed? Why does the president finally, after all this time, give you what you're looking for in this area after almost everybody is gone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you used a very good term that is appropriate, and I don't see any point in proclaiming a state of war there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know why it was done?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would this state of war make it much easier for the army to use the services of the civil protection services in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, civilian protection is a separate service. It is not under the jurisdiction of the army and that's the case all around the world. Members of the civilian protection are not armed. They have badges in the form of a triangle with the point upwards, and I think it's the colour yellow. And I think that everybody should respect this service because they are providing for the needs of the vulnerable population. Now, if your question was whether it was easier for the army to carry out its duties under such circumstances, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Civil protection can also do asanacija, cleaning up the battle-field of human and other animal remains and bury them to prevent diseases; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And since, like you say, they are a civilian organisation not attached to the army, this decree requires them to give the army what they want, if the army wants them to do asanacija or something else; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if Colonel Beara on the night of the 13th met with the head of civil protection or the other civil authorities and asked them for help to bury bodies, they would not be obliged by this decree because it doesn't come into play until the next day, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it wouldn't be binding. But they have their ongoing tasks, the civilian protection. Their ongoing tasks during a war is to carry out these jobs that you mentioned and enumerated very nicely in your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The Court has heard evidence in this case that on the 14th of July, as a result of mass executions at the Kravica warehouse, their civil protection assisted - with the urging of Colonel Beara and others - in burying, digging holes and burying the dead on 14 July. So if civil protection was working with the army on the 14th of July, and the 15th of July, this decree would have been in place at that time, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can Mr. McCloskey give the proper reference to the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question was my question. I think it's been repeated in this trial unknown how many times, the digging of the graves at Glogova on the 14th of July. Colonel Beara's involvement with the civil protection. The graves were continued to be dug on the 15th July. All I am asking him is whether or not the army was able to take advantage of this proclamation that required the help of civil protection in that effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. They could have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, let me try to get to it. We'll go to a topic that's a little bit more related to structure, a little away from digging for a moment. The -- you spoke a bit about the 410th and the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And you, I think, correctly pointed out that they were units directly connected to General Mladic, the commander. And right near the end of the -- your answers to those, you did say the 410th was not part of the intel and security. They were a separate unit. But you did go on to say, on 18566, when you were asked: "Did the commander exercise command and control over this body," meaning the 410th. And your answer is: "He did exercise command, that's for sure. But perhaps he transferred certain authorities to the sector for intelligence and security." This Court has heard quite a bit of evidence on the 410th and especially the 10th Sabotage Detachment being, like you have said, under the command of General Mladic. But, as you, I think, have told us, and we have heard otherwise, General Mladic is a very busy man and, of course, he can't follow the day-to-day management, "rukovodjenje," if we might put it that way, of these units. So when you say Mladic has transferred certain authorities over to the sector of intelligence and security, can you tell us is that true, do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. McCloskey. And I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would that have been the same thing, that it's true that he transferred certain authorities over to the intelligence and security section regarding the 10th Sabotage Detachment as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 07601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what about the last document, 65 ter 677?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I should offer that into evidence if it is not, 677. Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2869. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this 07601 is something we identified in response to the general's answers to General Tolimir about the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and so I would wish to have this on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is my understanding that Mr. Tolimir never objects to this kind of request. Leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could -- if that's up on the screen for the general, and we could make it a bit easier because I -- sorry, I see I am running out of time. Could we provide that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you have indicated that you will need six hours. That time-limit is not reached yet. Of course, we should try to conclude the testimony of this witness today, that's for sure, but as was the same for Mr. Tolimir, there is no time pressure. Mr. Tolimir should have enough time for his re-examination. During the break, we could consider to have an extended hearing today. The courtroom is available in the afternoon. That would be one option. You have up to now used 3 hours and 48 minutes. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Take your time or we continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was hoping to finish, but I am now recognising I'm in some important areas. So thank you for understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, general. Just take a read of this as you will. And we'll flip over the next page in a while so that General Tolimir can read it fully, but it's a document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's basically an order from General Mladic on 4 December 1994, to the organs of the security and intel affairs on all levels from battalion to the Main Staff of the VRS shall commence with a selection of personnel in accordance with the requirements below. And it's -- as we see in the title, it's regarding the establishing and recruiting the Main Staff 10th Sabotage Detachment. This is clearly a personnel issue. It's when you were working. So it's basically ordering - as we all know he has the right and authority to do - to get these units together to properly recruit and get the 10th Sabotage Detachment going and get personnel for it. Is that basically it in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7601 shall be assigned Exhibit P2870. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to P2141.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a much simpler one-page document from the Main Staff, 21 December 1994. So over two weeks after General Mladic's order. We'll flip that around for you. Blow it up a bit. You will see it's from the intel and security centre from General Tolimir. And it's entitled: "Warning, re: The selection of the candidates of the Main Staff 10th Sabotage Detachment." And it refers to the communication from Mladic, and that's the same that we just saw, just so you know. And we see General Tolimir saying he received an order from the commander with a dead-line. Selecting candidates to be accepted on contract into the Main Staff 10th Sabotage Detachment. And he says: "Since you have not taken any action in this matter up till now, nor have you sent this sector any report, I hereby warn you to take this task extremely seriously and to begin realising it through your subordinate organs up to the battalion level." Is this an example of General Tolimir implementing the order of his commander in the area of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's an example, only I don't see to whom it is addressed. You don't see the name of the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we go back to the document he is referring to, we can see who that one was sent to. But I would -- that's already in evidence. So we see here, don't we, that on this particular date General Tolimir has some management authority and involvement with the 10th Sabotage Detachment in terms of its formation and getting it together?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you agree with me on that, this shows that General Tolimir has involvement as the chief of intel and security with the management of the 10th Sabotage situation? In this case, the formation of its personnel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. But he was not responsible for the formation. That was part of my sector's duty. He was only in charge of providing good quality personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was in charge of getting the security people's attention so they followed Mladic's order - right? - as he is doing in this document? Nobody had done anything for two weeks and --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Tolimir let them have it. One last question. The Mladic document we see, the order to get personnel, and then the Tolimir document we see implementing that, can we say that the Mladic document is a good example of "komandovanje" and the Tolimir document is a good example of "rukovodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whether it's a command or a "rukovodjenje," the people that are on the other side of these communications have to do what they are told to do, don't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that, first of all, they didn't do what they had been told to do, and then the general reminded them that they had to take action. And I probably reminded the individuals who were to act in a certain document. I probably told them to accelerate the preparations for having contracts drawn up with members of the 2nd -- members of the 10th Detachment. But in answer to your question my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is no doubt in your mind whatsoever, is there, that they'd acted on Tolimir's reminder? Or warning, as he called it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt in my mind but they worked slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We inquired, in the meantime, if it would be possible to have an extended third session today, that means from 1.00 to 2.30. We didn't get a response from the relevant people yet, because this involves interpreters and the whole support staff. We will let the parties know as soon as possible as we get this information, at least at the beginning of the next session. We must have our second break now and will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is very grateful for the staff who is now prepared to sit until 2.30 today, but just to make it clear to both parties, there is no time pressure at all. We can try to finish the testimony of this witness today. If it is not possible because there are remaining questions, especially in re-examination, we can continue on Monday. Just to let you know how things stand. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to D248.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document that the Defence has introduced. It's a -- it's entitled: "Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces," general, 1987. So I think you will see it's an old JNA document. There's the front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 24 in the B/C/S and page 18 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this should be the chapter entitled: "Organisation of Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces," and I just want to ask you about this -- it's paragraph 14 that you see up there. "The intelligence organ of the superior command staff of the armed forces directs and co-ordinates the expert work of the intelligence and reconnaissance organs and reconnaissance units in directly subordinate commands, staffs and units, provides expert assistance, and controls their overall intelligence and reconnaissance activity." Was this basic rule used in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on to another subject briefly. You spoke about rather important topic briefly. It was on page 18541 [Realtime transcript read in error "48451"]. And the general asked you: "Since you were an assistant commander in both the Main Staff and at the corps level, can you tell us whether the assistant commander at the Main Staff could issue orders to assistant commanders at the corps level; in other words, did they have command ability or capability?" And your answer was: "No." Now, of course, as I think you have reiterated and I have agreed, we know that assistant commanders are not commanders and they don't have command ability, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But as we've already seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 64, line 22, I think the page of the transcript noted down is erroneous. We haven't yet reached that page, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope we will never reach that in this trial, Mr. Gajic. I don't know if the -- now the microphone is working. That's true, but that will be corrected. You see the sign after the page number. And the Registrar found the relevant page. Mr. McCloskey, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we agree on that, but as you've seen, we have seen an example of General Tolimir speaking in documents to his subordinate assistants. So I want to see if we can just clarify that because it slightly muddied the way that question was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's go now to 65 ter 7556. And this is a document with a new 65 ter number that we brought up in response to this very important issue, and it is a two-page document. It may be easier if the -- if the witness had both pages, though the second page is only a few lines. And for the benefit of everyone, the English is also two pages, but this is from Chief Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. So if we -- and it's taking this issue back in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we see, this is a -- it goes back into at least December of 1992. But it's from the VRS, at that time, administration for intelligence and security affairs, entitled: "Procedure with Prisoners of War in the Manjaca POW Camp." And it's General Tolimir again, as we have seen him do on July 9th, 1995, he is passing on or saying something relating to a decision by President Karadzic. And we see here that he says President Karadzic has decided to disband the Manjaca LRZ on 25 December 1992, Catholic Christmas, as a token of goodwill and in order to reduce the tensions among the international general public caused by nonobjective reporting about the LRZ situation in the Republika Srpska. He will announce his decision via the media. And now this is what General Tolimir is telling to, as we see, the 1st Krajina Corps, the department for intelligence and security, personally, to Bogdanovic, regarding the procedures for prisoners of war. After the decision has been publicly announced, all prisoners in the Manjaca LRZ will be handed over to the ICRC and will leave our state in a way that they organise. However, our position that we cannot release certain number of Croats because of the large number of our soldiers in Croatian camps, as well as extremist Muslims and Muslims against whom criminal reports have been submitted for serious criminal offences and crimes against humanity has been respected by President Karadzic. In accordance with this, it is necessary that you proceed as follows. And now he's directing people as we can see. By 15 December 1992, investigate and report whether you have a suitable place in your zone for the relocation and accomodation of the aforesaid categories of prisoners of war. With respect to the Muslims for whom you have operational and technical documentation that they have comitted serious crimes, crimes against humanity, and for whom you possess information that they are extremist and will rejoin their hostile formations on being released, and against whom you have not submitted criminal reports, do so immediately. Also separate these Muslims and prepare to relocate them and accommodate them outside the Manjaca camp. So it goes on on the second page. It talks about carry out the above with full secrecy measures. I won't go through the rest of it, but it does underline at the end: "In the event of any lack of clarity in this telegram, contact Colonel Tolimir or Captain First-Class Pecanac." Now, this is clearly a direction, isn't it, of General Tolimir to the intel and security department of the 1st Krajina Corps for, among other things, to separate the potential war criminals from the group going to the ICRC and hold them? Very directive in nature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are instructions, directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is not "komandovanje" but it's "rukovodjenje," this assistant commander at the 1st Krajina Corps has to do what Tolimir tells him to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, these are professional instructions. The assistant of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps has to show these instructions to the commander. The commander of the 1st Krajina Corps or all the other corps who receive this - but this was addressed only to the 1st Corps -- should I slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't quite hear the interpreter very well, but it doesn't hurt to slow down. We are all probably getting a little tired.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology. The interpreter will try to speak more loudly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Please carry on with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me be brief. The assistant commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, upon receiving such instructions or directions, has the duty of making the corps commander aware of the fact. He has to suggest measures to him, and when he received the authorisation from the corps commander, then he can implement the instructions in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can or must?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Must.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just as I -- I see this thing at the end. Basically it says in the event of clarity, contact Tolimir or First Class Pecanac. Is that Captain First Class Pecanac the same Pecanac that was part of the Main Staff in 1995? I think you put him in one of the little boxes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, Mr. McCloskey. And I am pretty certain that it is the same person. If his name was Dragomir in addition to that, then I would be completely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, Dragomir Pecanac stayed as a captain, either a captain first class or a captain, throughout the entire war, but yet he remained in the Main Staff in a fairly trusted position. Can you tell us why -- why so little promotion for Mr. Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he was promoted to the rank of major just before the end of the war. I don't remember exactly. But in the Main Staff he was part of the personal security for the Main Staff commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7556 shall be assigned Exhibit P2871. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And another document on this same point, 65 ter 3840. And this is a two-page document which -- and again, I am not at the point where I want to go through all the details of this, but just fundamentally what it is, but to the degree that it will be easier for you to see what it is in two pages. It is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, intelligence and security sector, on 27 January 1994. Again, it is from Assistant Commander Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, entitled: "Providing Security for a Military and Political Consultation." And it talks about on order of the deputy commander of the Main Staff of the Army of RS, and it talks about security measures for people in Vlasenica at the Hotel Panorama. And it says "Order." And we can see that it is an order to the 5th Military Police Battalion from the Drina Corps to assign an officer. And it's a very particularised order and it won't in through all of it, guard posts and things. And then it goes to the commander of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment shall assign one officer and others and gives them very particular orders, including six military policemen, as well as a whole series of specific orders. As we get to the second -- second page in English, second page in B/C/S that I won't go over. Paragraph 7 near the bottom -- at the bottom of the page it talks about: "I hereby assign Captain First Class Dragomir Pecanac to carry out this order." So we clearly now have an order from General Tolimir regarding security, military police forces, and all. So, is this, in his position, his "rukovodjenje" or is he in some kind of command position now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it was part of "rukovodjenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is implementing the order of the -- of the deputy commander by developing his own orders consistent with that, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3840 shall be assigned Exhibit P2872. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I have similar documents, Your Honour, going up to 95, but that the Court has seen over and over again, so I think my point is made clear. So I will go to my last area because those documents that I would ask him about are in evidence and I think are pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you in speaking with General Tolimir spoke -- you both spoke at length about these drones that NATO had that were -- you, yourself, I think may have seen them. And you described how they, as far as you knew, were taking pictures of an area, and that you had -- you would agree with me that these were a potential -- let me take you to July 1995, when you had been bombed by NATO, both, I think, in May and in July, around Srebrenica. I won't go into the whole hostage crisis, but we have drones flying around your combat areas of Srebrenica and Zepa. This is an extreme intelligence threat and security threat for the forces that could be photographed and potentially bombed by NATO aircraft, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so any significant military operation that was taking place in the areas around Srebrenica, Zepa, and Zvornik, these drones were a serious potential security problem for your people, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not just a security problem but a general problem because they could gather information in various ways. And this information could be placed at the disposal of all those interested in it, apart from the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It could also potentially -- NATO could have potentially released photographs to the media, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also a possibility, Mr. McCloskey. I didn't notice that, but it's possible and in technical terms it's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when Madeleine Albright did just that on the floor of the United Nations? It was in August 1995, showed pictures from in and around the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. But it was described as being -- or they were described as being satellite photographs, but it's not important. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go to P124. And my previous -- all right. Let me just let you take a look at that. This is 14 July, a date we're, well, very familiar with in many respects now. And we see that it's from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade which, as you know, is in Rogatica. And you can -- well, you can't see it right now, but it's in the name of General Tolimir. And I want to take you to the -- what's the second page in English and almost near the bottom of the document in the B/C/S. And it says: "Early this morning, since 0500 hours, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Plbpr," as we know is the Rogatica Brigade, "and above the Muslim enclaves of Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde, there is an unmanned aerial vehicle whose flight path we can determine only by sound. "It is probably recording the positions and movement of units. Radio communication interference is registered. The orders for camouflage measures and organisation of multiple communications systems have been issued." So is it clear from this that on the 14th of July - we see this is handwritten around 1045 hours - that in the morning General Tolimir is fully aware of the threat of photography from, in this particular case, a drone in the areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir could have drawn the conclusion as to what the results would be of this aerial reconnaissance. And what the results would be of having taken these aerial photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this he is passing on the information that orders for camouflage measures and organisations of multiple communications system has been issued. So he is passing on the fact that action has been taken regarding this threat, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, only it's not quite clear to me why a letter from the brigade is linked to a signature of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't know that General Tolimir had been sent by Mladic as he is -- tends to do when big operations are present to have a Main Staff officer on the ground helping co-ordinate with General Krstic in this case, or others? That practice was fully laid out in the 1992 report that you referred to earlier. So you weren't aware that General Tolimir was sent down to that area at that time to help out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, General Mladic sent each and every one of us to various tasks. Therefore, I am not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go to another document. It's P121. This is a -- another document from the Rogatica Brigade, dated 14 July, and General Tolimir's name. There is a stamp on it, 1845. So it appears to be a few hours after the previous document. And its strictly confidential number is 520-54 and the previous one was 520-53. So in this one we have coming out from General Tolimir from the command of the Rogatica Brigade all subordinate units of the Drina Corps. And if we see the back of this one, the next page in English, we can see that it has a stamp of the Zvornik Brigade, so they received it. And in this document to all the brigades, it points out that: "There is an unmanned aircraft in the air-space reconnoitring and jamming radio communications. Since the aircraft has been there since 0500 hours this morning and has probably taken pictures of certain features and movements, the following needs to be done." And it talks about various things Tolimir is saying should be done, alerting people. Maintain all radio communications. Number 4: "If spotted, the unmanned aircraft should be immediately destroyed." So this is a clear order from Tolimir to destroy this aircraft, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a clear order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that ordering the shoot-down of a NATO aircraft who is potentially and most probably photographing what's going on on the ground in the area of the Drina Corps is a rather significant order in terms of General Tolimir's position and the situation you were facing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, members of the aircraft defence do not have to wait for anyone's order. If they spot the target, an enemy target, call it what you will, there is no need for them to await an order from anyone. Their duty is to destroy it if they have the resources for that. But we didn't have such resources to destroy unmanned aircrafts in high altitudes. We didn't have missile units in that area. We only had artillery units that had weapons that had a range of up to 3.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the VRS at that time had carte blanche to fire on any NATO aircraft, manned or unmanned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Please, this is a representation claiming that this is an order issued by Tolimir, and I think that it should be put to the witness that this is an order only passed on by Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may deal with this in your re-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, general, given that the troops on the ground, as you say, had the ability to shoot this down without orders, General Tolimir would have had the ability to issue such an order even without Mladic's approval, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who would General Tolimir need to be in communication with on this point before sending this order out on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will go back to my original question: Is this order, be it directly from Mladic through Tolimir or Tolimir on his own - I will take him at his word it's coming from Mladic - this is a significant order to do a significant thing, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if General Tolimir on the 14th of July had knowledge that thousands of able-bodied men were being transported visibly in vehicles from Bratunac to Zvornik, and being assembled in schools around the Zvornik area, and being taken out that afternoon and summarily executed, an order to prevent any potential photographing of those operations and activities would be a significant part of such an operation, to cover up this crime, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask Mr. McCloskey to give us a reference. Where does it say that I knew about this? And then it would be relevant, just like the first sentence is not clearly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey started his question by the words, "So if General Tolimir ..." and so on. You may raise this question with the witness in your re-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, general? I can simplify it: If General Tolimir knew that there was this very visible operation to transport thousands of people up to Zvornik that could be photographed by this thing, this is a significant order to shoot it out of the sky so it couldn't do it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you about the motives, Mr. McCloskey, because anti-aircraft defence's task is to destroy targets marked with an X. I didn't speak about NATO aircraft at all. And there is a service within anti-aircraft defence that marks such targets and they are legitimate targets that can be fired at. However, we all in our minds can connect the dots between various events which might logically seem correct. However, your supposition that this has to do with the digging or whatever you referred to, I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me that from these two documents we can tell that General Tolimir is naturally concerned about NATO taking photographs above the Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa areas for natural military reasons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, that was the case throughout the whole territory over which drones flew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if those -- if that drone or those drones flew over the positions of General or Colonel Pandurevic's troops as they were going into Zepa, and later on, as it flew up to Zvornik showed the movement of Muslim prisoners from a school to a field nearby, both such activities on the ground would give General Tolimir good cause to blow that thing out of the sky? Not that he's doing it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about General Tolimir, but I think that would be a reasonable conclusion for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One last -- last area in response to something General Tolimir said. If we have the situation we have from a period of 13, 14, 15, 16 July, the steady and constant summary execution of 6.000 able-bodied men between Bratunac and Pilica, could such a thing occur without superior orders from the highest levels of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to? The destruction of aircraft? Can you please repeat your question, and if possible, please, can you be a little more brief so that I can follow you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could 6.000 able-bodied Muslim men be butchered over a four-day period by the VRS without orders from the highest levels of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no order to kill people, regardless of the figure that is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did those over 6.000, 7.000 men get murdered in four days without orders from on high?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I am not a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General Skrbic, for all your time. And I know it's a tough spot to be in, and I don't have any further questions on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before Mr. Tolimir gets the floor for his re-examination, I have one question for the witness. Sir, you will remember that during your examination-in-chief you were asked about your war diary. This is D350, marked for identification. It started -- the entry started on the 18th of March and it ends somewhere in May, if I am not mistaken, 1995. Today you told us -- and you told us the day before that later on you didn't take any notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Today, this is transcript page 42, lines 11 through 16. You said the following, I quote: "In Belgrade, I, in fact, told you that I made certain notes on my computer and these notes were made from memory, and it is on that basis that I drew the conclusion that I must have been there on the 14th or around that date because of that decree that concerned the retirement of General Zivanovic and the appointment of certain other generals." When did you take these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the entire war, Your Honour, I took notes that referred to personnel issues and organisations. And these notes that you referred to, operative notes, were without the scope of my responsibility, and I said that this kind of operative notes I did not keep after May. And I am talking about intelligence notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And these notes about matters of your area of responsibility, you wrote down on your computer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Tolimir, please, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In order for us to complete within the working hours, could we please start with Exhibit P121.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skrbic, take a look at line 1 of this document, and can you tell me whether this order that you see here had come from the Main Staff of the VRS and then passed on by the signatory of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry for not waiting for the interpretation to finish, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was this order then issued by the Main Staff or by Tolimir? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tolimir, this is a little bit a leading question, but one can see that this was issued by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During combat operations, was it legitimate to destroy NATO drones in our air-space?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as NATO took sides and sided with the opposite side, it became legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, I just stopped you because when you finished your question, the translation was not finished yet. Please don't overlap between question and answer. Now your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, was the activity of anti-aircraft defence systems of the VRS legitimate in these instances and was it ordered by the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I am not a lawyer. Therefore, I am not able to tell you whether something is legitimate or not legitimate. However, the anti-aircraft defence of Republika Srpska had an ongoing order to shoot down enemy flying aircraft, starting from drones and other aircraft, if found in their air-space and provided they had technical capability for that. But as for legitimacy, please don't ask me to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Skrbic, for all your answers. Thank you for coming to testify here. I wish you a long life and success in your retirement period. And on behalf of the Defence team, I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions because we want to abide by the allocated time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you will be aware of the fact that we have an extended time available until 2.30. If you have more questions, you are entitled to put these to the witness, but it's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understand what you told me, but the Defence has no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Sir, this concludes your testimony in this trial. You are now free to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for the assistance you were able to give us in our tasks. Thank you very much. We have to adjourn and we will resume on Monday at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1.54 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of February, 2012, at 2.15 p.m.
